articles.title: Opinion - When history reckons with Donald Trump, it won’t forget America’s role
articles.summary: Someday each of us will be asked the question, “What did you do when people were killed on the streets?"
articles.body:
Dylan Corbett, executive director of the Hope Border Institute, recently told the National Catholic Reporter that we are going through " a dark night of the soul as a country ."

Just last month, several children gathered in a courtroom to have their futures decided by a Texas judge. One was a six-year-old who pretended to fly an airplane; another was a three-year-old who played with a microphone. They were among 25 minors facing deportation hearings that day.

Angel was one of them. Just 13 years old, he pleaded that it was "too dangerous" to be returned to Honduras, adding, "My mom and my entire family are here." The judge ruled that Angel did not qualify for asylum and asked whether he wanted either a deportation order or would leave voluntarily. At that, Angel burst into tears crying : "I have no one. I have nothing."

The stories of those young Texas children are not the only examples of the cruelties inflicted upon immigrants by the Trump administration.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have murdered U.S. citizens and patrol our streets. Children wonder whether their parents will be home when they return from school. And many immigrants who have followed the rules are being deported not to their home countries, but to places like South Sudan, Eswatini and Rwanda .

Earlier this year , Renée Good and Alex Pretti became household names when they were publicly executed on the streets of Minneapolis. In Biddeford, Maine, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a food delivery worker, was killed by an ICE officer in front of his wife and three-year-old daughter. Houston, Texas, saw Lorenzo Salgado Araujo gunned down by ICE agents as he was on his way to a job at a construction site.

During the past year, 37 people have died in ICE custody, many with Hispanic surnames whose identities are not household names but are known to God.

At a Catholic mass held for the World Day of Migrants and Refugees, Washington, D.C., Cardinal Robert McElroy recited the story of the Good Samaritan. In it, Jesus Christ describes a priest and Levite who saw a robbery victim laying on the side of the road and passed by. Only the Samaritan stopped, treated the victim's wounds, and paid for his stay at a nearby inn.

As Cardinal McElroy noted , it's easy to dislike the priest and the Levite, and admire the Good Samaritan.

When migrants are deported, raids on farm workers and Home Depots take place and mothers and children are detained, many of us have assumed the role of the priest and Levite and passed on by.

When the Trump administration dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development, which has saved millions of lives overseas, many wondered, "What can we do?"

Donald Trump has called himself " the greatest president ever ." Scholars disagree. Steven Levitsky, a professor of government at Harvard University, contends that during Trump's second term in office the U.S. has "slid into some form of authoritarianism."

Americans are equally disenchanted with Trump. An Economist/YouGov poll finds hefty majorities describe him as "arrogant," "opportunistic," "reckless," "dishonest," "corrupt," "hypocritical" and "divisive."

It is easy to characterize the past decade as the era of Trumpism, a word that encompasses the cruelties inflicted by Trump, the degradation of our political institutions and attacks on the rule of law.

Using a word to describe a political era happened once before during the 1950s, when Sen. Joseph McCarthy (R-Wisc.) charged that the U.S. government had been infiltrated by communist sympathizers. Harry Truman declared that McCarthy's only importance was that his name "has taken on a dictionary meaning".

"It is the rise to power of the demagogue who lives on untruth; it is the spreading of fear and destruction of faith in every level of our society."

Truman's definition of McCarthyism can be applied to the word Trumpism. But the danger is that like the 1950s, we will look upon this present moment and blame one man who used his power for nefarious purposes. Someday each of us will be asked the question, "What did you do when people were killed on the streets, or children held in detention, or when other cruelties too numerous to mention were inflicted on others?"

Did you, as Cardinal McElroy said, " pass on by "? Or will you be able to say that you protested, voted or otherwise made your views known?

In his 1953 inaugural address , Dwight D. Eisenhower offered "a little private prayer" to the Almighty: "Give us, we pray, the power to discern clearly right from wrong, and allow all our words and actions to be governed thereby, and by the laws of this land."

He asked for cooperation to be the goal for those who "hold to differing political faiths; so that all may work for the good of our beloved country and Thy Glory."

This too, should be our prayer. A historical reckoning with Trump is coming.

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled " Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics. "

articles.title: Mass. Lt. Gov. candidate hit 5 parked cars and flipped SUV before arrest on OUI charge, police report says
articles.summary: Police say a former Massachusetts government lieutenant candidate was bleeding, glassy-eyed and smelled of alcohol after flipping his SUV on Dartmouth Street...
articles.body:
The former Massachusetts lieutenant governor-hopeful who was arrested in connection with drunken driving on Saturday night appeared in New Bedford court on Monday morning.

Shawn Oliver, 42, is facing charges of operating under the influence (OUI) of alcohol in addition to motor vehicles charges of negligent operation, marked lanes violation and speeding, according to charging documents in his case.

Oliver pleaded not guilty and was ordered released on personal recognizance from New Bedford District Court on Monday morning by Judge Joseph Harrington Jr. He is scheduled to appear again on Nov. 16.

Oliver is a current New Bedford city councilor and Bristol County House of Corrections officer who was running on the ticket as a Republican candidate with Mike Minogue against current Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll and Gov. Maura Healey. He announced he was suspending his campaign at around 2 p.m. on Sunday, less than 24 hours after his arrest Saturday night and after Minogue had called on him to do so Sunday morning.

"After careful reflection, I have made the decision to suspend my campaign for Lieutenant Governor," Oliver, who was running as a Republican in the race, said in a statement released at 2:17 p.m. on Sunday.

"This election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters. I want to sincerely thank everyone who has supported me throughout this journey and ask that my family's privacy be respected during this difficult time," Oliver said.

Oliver's attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Monday.

According to three New Bedford police reports on the incident, Oliver was driving a black Lincoln Navigator north on Dartmouth Street at around 11:30 p.m., just south of the Rockdale Avenue intersection.

A witness who spoke to officers at the scene said he was stopped in his own car behind Oliver's Navigator at an intersection light on Dartmouth Street. When the light turned green, the witness said the Navigator did not pull forward.

After a few moments sitting at the light — and the witness reversing his own car to view that the light was green — the Navigator suddenly accelerated forward and drifted to the right, almost hitting the curb by New York Bagel at 571 Dartmouth St., the report read.

The Navigator then "abruptly" veered to the left to avoid striking the curb, the report read, and continued onward. After crossing through the Dartmouth and Rockdale intersection, the Navigator again drifted to the left and crossed over the yellow center line.

Police say Oliver struck five parked cars and was driving so fast that he flipped his Navigator upside down onto its roof.

Oliver was outside of the car and standing on the sidewalk, speaking on his cellphone when officers arrived at the scene, the report read. A bystander brought out a chair and officers told Oliver to sit down, noting that he was bleeding from an injury on the right side of his head.

Oliver repeatedly asked officers at the scene if "everyone else was OK," though they told him he was the only person involved in the crash, the report read. Oliver also told officers he was "burning both ends of the wick," and said he "was coming from a meeting with friends in Dartmouth."

Oliver was unable to complete a field sobriety test due to his injuries and was brought to the hospital, where he then told officers he'd drank at least two alcoholic beverages earlier in the night at Black Bass Grill. He then had gone to a friend's house located in Dartmouth, police said.

Oliver's eyes were "bloodshot and glassy," he was emanating "a moderate odor of alcoholic beverages" and he vomited at the hospital before he was placed under arrest.

"After speaking with Shawn, it was determined that he was under the influence of alcoholic beverages therefore should not have been operating a motor vehicle," the report read.

"At this point he was advised that he was being placed under arrest and was handcuffed to the hospital bed," the report read. Oliver refused to have his blood drawn at the hospital.

articles.title: Ro Khanna sparks backlash over France riot comments as critic says he wants to ‘ride the rage wave’
articles.summary: Ro Khanna argued France riots show a need to "listen to our young," drawing sharp backlash from critics who accused him of excusing political violence.
articles.body: Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a potential 2028 presidential contender, drew criticism from across the political spectrum after pointing to the riots in France as a warning about wealth inequality and urging the U.S. to "listen to our young." "This is what happens when the nations let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few," Khanna wrote in a post to X on Sunday evening. Khanna's post comes on the heels of nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living and public services that descended into violence, looting and arson in several French cities on Saturday, prompting critics to accuse the progressive Democrat of giving political legitimacy to the destruction. Spencer Pratt, former mayoral candidate for Los Angeles, blasted what he saw as an attempt to side with rioters. JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIALISM IS BACK IN STYLE AND DEMOCRATS ARE BUYING THE PITCH "Of course Rohit Conman sees mass communist riots destroying businesses and historic buildings in Paris and lies about it as some noble ‘ask’ for justice," Pratt wrote. "These commies lie as easily as they breathe." The comment also drew criticism from Shannon Watts, a Democratic gun activist who, in recent months, has criticized the far-left portions of her party. "If you’re a member of Congress who condemned the January 6 insurrection, you don’t get to excuse riots in France as a ‘cry for help.’ Political violence doesn’t become acceptable just because you sympathize with people committing it," Watts wrote in a post of her own. Still others warned Khanna against using the moment as a way to build political momentum. "Ro Khanna has long sought to ride the rage wave to power," Jonathan Turley, a political commentator and legal analyst, said. "Khanna could indeed learn much from France. This is history repeating itself. That history, by the way, does not bode well for establishment figures who pander to the mob," Turley added, giving a nod to the infamous French Revolution that targeted the country’s political and financial elite in a bloody crusade. Planned demonstrations in France over the weekend quickly spiraled out of control on Saturday, leaving behind broken storefronts and fires in Paris. French authorities said that by Sunday evening they had arrested nearly 2,400 people nationwide, including 855 in the Paris region. Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, seven seriously, according to France's Interior Ministry. One protester died after suffering cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris, authorities said. WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED In Limoges, a fire that authorities said was deliberately set at the city hall caused significant damage to the historic building. Shops were looted in Paris, Bordeaux, Marseille, Lyon and other cities, while public buildings were vandalized or targeted by fires. Authorities estimated that more than 550,000 people participated in demonstrations across France. Organizers put the figure at roughly 800,000. Despite the mayhem, Khanna argued the moment should prompt American lawmakers to take younger voters' political demands more seriously, especially on topics of equity. "This is what happens when young people lose hope in their future. In America, let us listen to our young. We need an economic and political transformation. America’s Next New Deal," Khanna wrote. "From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in," Khanna wrote. But in the face of the backlash online, Khanna quickly clarified his stance in a follow-up post, noting that he did not support the destruction that had unfolded. "I unequivocally condemn violence and vandalism. I have always championed my grandfather’s example of non-violent protest," Khanna wrote, referencing his relative, Amarnath Vidyalankar, who was imprisoned for advocating for India’s independence in the early 1930s. "Let us not be blind to the anger young people have against the unholy alliance of wealth and power. The billionaires buying politicians. The corruption," Khanna added. But even after issuing his clarifying statement, Khanna continued to face condemnation — even from figures like former Rep. George Santos, R-N.Y. "These are not mere students… my friend, I regret to inform you, this is an invasion," Santos wrote, referring to France’s high intake of refugees in recent years. Khanna, responding to Santos, doubled down on his view. BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP "George, is the lesson not to tackle the vast disparity here and young people’s hopelessness?" he asked. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Khanna’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital. Bradford Benz contributed to this report

articles.title: Trump threatened by judge with sanctions if he doesn’t sit for deposition in $10 billion BBC defamation suit
articles.summary: The BBC filed a motion to compel Donald Trump's deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit, and a magistrate judge now warns of sanctions.
articles.body: President Donald Trump was threatened by a judge with sanctions if he doesn’t sit for a deposition in the $10 billion defamation lawsuit he filed against the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC). Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC late last year for its 2024 "Panorama" documentary that distorted his remarks to supporters on Jan. 6, 2021. Critics claim the documentary was misleading because it omitted Trump's call for supporters to protest peacefully, splicing together separate portions of a lengthy address to give a wrong impression. But Trump has been too busy to sit for a deposition, and the BBC said the president’s legal team insisted "has no availability whatsoever" before the end of the discovery period on Dec. 18 because he is busy dealing with "matters of national importance." TRUMP FILES 'POWERHOUSE' $10 BILLION LAWSUIT AGAINST BBC OVER DOCUMENTARY EDITING HIS JAN 6 REMARKS As a result, the BBC filed a motion to compel Trump’s deposition. The BBC has said it understands that Trump’s deposition requires "additional planning," and he "accepted the obligations of civil litigation" when he chose to file the lawsuit. "The Court has admonished Plaintiff for his lack of participation to no avail. Going forward, the Court expects strict compliance with its 29 Order, the failure of which will lead to sanctions," Magistrate Judge Enjolique A. Lett said on Friday, scheduling a hearing by Oct. 22. When asked for comment, Trump’s legal team blasted the British broadcaster. "The formerly respected and now disgraced BBC defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election. The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda. President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing," a spokesperson for his legal team told Fox News Digital. LEGAL ANALYST PREDICTS TRUMP COULD WIN 'CONSIDERABLE' DAMAGES FROM BBC DOCUMENTARY LAWSUIT The BBC declined a request for comment. Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in December in a personal capacity for both defamation and for a violation of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act for $5 billion apiece, seeking $10 billion total. The documentary omitted Trump urging his supporters to protest "peacefully" and instead spliced two separate comments made nearly an hour apart, making him appear he was calling for violence. "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And I'll be there with you. And we fight — we fight like hell," the documentary showed Trump saying. In reality, Trump said, "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you'll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong." It wasn't until 54 minutes later that Trump called on his supporters to "fight like hell" for election integrity. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The New York Times referred to the ordeal as "one of the worst crises in its 103-year history" of the BBC. The controversy led to the resignations of BBC News CEO Deborah Turness and BBC director-general Tim Davie. The BBC previously issued an apology for the erroneous edit and said it had pulled the program from its platforms. Despite the apology, the broadcaster has insisted the mistake is not enough for a defamation claim. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Joseph A. Wulfson contributed to this report.

articles.title: France's massive intel failure sparks resignation offers amid days of rioting
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron ordered a security review after France's intelligence services badly underestimated protests that overwhelmed 60,000 police officers.
articles.body: France is confronting a major intelligence failure after authorities badly underestimated the scale of nationwide protests that descended into riots and looting. The days of chaos have prompted French President Emmanuel Macron to order a security review as senior officials acknowledged police "lost control" in several major cities and senior government officials have offered to resign after they failed to predict the level of pandemonium. Some 550,000 people joined 110 marches nationwide Saturday, according to France's Interior Ministry, far exceeding an intelligence estimate of roughly 200,000 demonstrators. Organizers put turnout even higher, at 800,000. Cars burned in the streets, more than 1,500 stores were reportedly ransacked or destroyed and public buildings were attacked across the country. In Limoges, rioters broke into and torched a 19th-century city hall that had survived both world wars, causing its roof to collapse. By Monday, the Louvre remained closed as student protesters blocked its entrances, extending the disruption into another day. TOP TOURIST DESTINATION IN THE WORLD SHUTS DOWN AMID VIOLENT PROTESTS The unrest overwhelmed some 60,000 police, gendarmes and other security personnel deployed nationwide. Nearly 1,000 law enforcement officers and firefighters were injured, at least 2,400 people were arrested and French authorities estimate some 3,000 businesses sustained damage. As crowds swelled, police were stretched across multiple flashpoints while groups of masked rioters smashed storefronts, set fires and clashed with security forces. In some cities, authorities were unable to keep looters from moving through commercial districts even as officers struggled to contain the larger demonstrations. By Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez was acknowledging what shopkeepers and residents had already witnessed. FRENCH NEWSPAPER RIPS MACRON AFTER RIOTS ERUPT ACROSS FRANCE: ‘INDELIBLE STAIN’ "Yes, Saturday, in certain large cities, we lost control," Nuñez said. He acknowledged a "lack of anticipation" ahead of the demonstrations and said authorities had underestimated not only the number of protesters but the violent groups that would exploit the unrest. Nuñez offered his resignation to Macron. The president refused it and instead ordered a review of what the Élysée described as failures in planning and intelligence, demanding an accounting of how authorities had been caught so badly off guard. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin was even more direct. "We unquestionably failed," Darmanin said, pointing specifically to intelligence and France's difficulty tracking and confronting the ultra-left. The failure is particularly striking because the unrest did not emerge without warning. The warning signs had been building for weeks. The unrest began in September with high school students protesting teacher shortages, deteriorating school buildings and other conditions in classrooms around Paris. The movement quickly spread nationwide, drawing teachers, labor unions and other groups frustrated by rising living costs and declining public services. Violence had already begun creeping into the demonstrations. Students set fires at schools, cars were torched and protesters clashed with riot police as authorities made thousands of arrests. French intelligence services were watching the shift. At an Oct. 1 government crisis meeting, intelligence officials assessed that the movement had reached a "tipping point" from school blockades toward urban violence and attributed its origins to the hard-left France Unbowed party and its allies, Reuters reported. Yet little more than two weeks later, authorities were caught off guard by the scale of what hit the streets. Saturday brought together students, trade unionists, Yellow Vest veterans and other groups under a loose "convergence of struggles." Hundreds of thousands marched peacefully, while smaller groups of masked rioters broke away, looting stores, setting fires and attacking police. The violence has since ignited a separate political fight over immigration. WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED President Donald Trump blamed the destruction on France's migration policies, writing Monday that "the migrants have taken over France" and urging the country to close its borders. Other right-wing political leaders across Europe have made similar arguments. French authorities, however, have not blamed immigrants for the violence. Macron and his government have instead accused ultra-left militants and criminals of exploiting demonstrations rooted largely in education, living costs and public services. The unrest is nevertheless intensifying a political battle already reshaping France ahead of its 2027 presidential election, giving the right fresh ammunition on immigration, crime and the government's ability to maintain public order. Marine Le Pen's National Rally has seized on the violence to argue that Macron's government has lost control of the country, while other figures on the French right have pushed for tougher policing and immigration restrictions. The images of burning buildings, ransacked stores and overwhelmed police are landing at a particularly vulnerable moment for France's political establishment. Macron cannot seek a third consecutive term in 2027, leaving an open presidential contest as voters increasingly identify immigration, security and purchasing power among the country's major political concerns. The riots have also widened a debate over whether the breakdown reflects a failure of policing, deeper economic and social grievances or years of government policy on immigration and integration — competing explanations that are likely to shape France's political fight long after the streets are cleared. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For Macron's government, the immediate question is more concrete: how security services that were already tracking an increasingly volatile protest movement still failed to anticipate the scale of Saturday's violence.

articles.title: Zelenskyy briefs bipartisan group of lawmakers amid backlash over Trump’s Russia deal
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president detailed disruptions to U.S. support during a bipartisan call.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with a bipartisan group of lawmakers on Monday and raised concerns about President Donald Trump's decision to waive key sanctions on Russia, as members of Congress push back against the president's moves to ease economic pressure on Moscow.

During the video call, Zelenskyy reported concerns over disruptions to U.S. intelligence sharing and the administration's decision to waive Russia sanctions. He also told lawmakers that critical Starlink services remained degraded, hindering Ukraine's ability to intercept drones from Moscow, according to a readout from Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

Blumenthal and Tillis led the meeting, which included members of both the House and the Senate.

"Funding Russia's war machine, disabling Ukraine's satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace," the senators wrote in a joint statement. "Trying to appease a murderous thug like Vladimir Putin will only prolong this war and bring greater casualties."

According to the readout, Zelenskyy also raised concerns about delays in the delivery of critical air-defense interceptors. "As a result of these disruptions, civilians — children — are dying," Blumenthal and Tillis said.

In his own social media post , Zelenskyy reiterated what he told lawmakers and said he has received "no explanation" from America on intelligence sharing and Starlink degradation.

"Without America, things would be much harder for us," Zelenskyy told lawmakers in the video.

The call comes days after Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions on Russia that were outlined in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act — which he signed last month — that was intended to pressure Moscow to end the war.

Trump also temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel earlier this month, in the president's latest effort to bring down prices ahead of the midterms. That decision drew bipartisan criticism, including from Blumenthal and Tillis, who joined other senators in calling for Trump to "immediately reverse course."

Zelenskyy also told lawmakers that he was willing to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, as Trump has proposed , if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to do the same, the senators said.

Speaking to reporters at the White House Monday, Trump defended his sanctions relief and accused Zelenskyy of standing in the way of ending the war.

"I'm supporting stopping war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said when asked about criticism that he was supporting Putin. "And frankly, Zelenskyy is not helping matter much. I think he doesn't want to stop it."

Trump also said he would be willing to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping without Zelenskyy to discuss ending the war, and suggested someone else should negotiate for Ukraine.

"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said when asked about the Ukrainian leader's criticism that he was on the wrong side of history. "Maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate."

When ask for comment, the White House pointed back to the president's remarks.

Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), who also participated in the meeting, said he assured Zelenskyy of Congress' continued support and stressed that Ukraine must be included in negotiations over its future.

"While Trump's oil handouts to Vladimir Putin undermine the war effort, I made clear on our call that Congress is determined to support the brave Ukrainian people in their fight for freedom," Durbin said. "Any negotiations about the future of Ukraine after years defending against Russian assault must include Ukraine."

Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump says he would be open to trilateral meeting with Putin, Xi
articles.summary: President Trump said Monday he has not yet agreed to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, but he said he is open to it. “I would do it,” Trump told reporters on the White House’s South Lawn before heading to a midterm rally in Kansas. “Not so much…
articles.body:
President Trump said Monday he has not yet agreed to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, but he said he is open to it.

“I would do it,” Trump told reporters on the White House’s South Lawn before heading to a midterm rally in Kansas.

“Not so much on Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine, they haven’t been doing much, and the same with China,” the president continued. “We would have it to talk about weapons and denuclearization.”

Trump’s comments came after The Wall Street Journal reported Putin proposed a trilateral meeting to discuss the war in Ukraine on a call with Trump earlier this month.

The call reportedly led to the U.S. president announcing he would waive sanctions on Russia to buy diesel from the country. Trump’s move was a part of an effort to lower diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections.

Trump also noted the leaders would likely talk about other issues like trade and suggested such a summit would likely be held in China.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded to reports about the potential summit, writing it would not be acceptable.

“A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US, and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war,” Sybiha wrote.

Zelensky has lashed out at Trump’s move to waive sanctions on Russia regarding diesel and has said his U.S. counterpart “is on the wrong side of history.” Trump responded to the criticism on Monday, saying the Ukrainian leader does not know what he is talking about.

“Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get someone else to negotiate,” Trump told reporters.

articles.title: 91 percent in Texas poll say Iran war raising oil and gas prices
articles.summary: More than 90 percent of Texas voters believe the Iran conflict is raising oil and gas prices, according to a new survey. In the CBS News/YouGov poll, 91 percent of respondents said the war against Iran is making oil and gas prices in the U.S. “a lot higher” or “a little higher.” Only 7 percent…
articles.body:
More than 90 percent of Texas voters believe the Iran conflict is raising oil and gas prices , according to a new survey.

In the CBS News/YouGov poll , 91 percent of respondents said the war against Iran is making oil and gas prices in the U.S. “a lot higher” or “a little higher.” Only 7 percent of Texas voters said the conflict is having “no impact” on oil and gas prices, while 1 percent said the conflict is making oil and gas prices “a little lower.”

The poll comes almost two weeks out from the 2026 midterm elections, in which energy prices are a central issue. The conflict against Iran — which is nearing the eight-month mark — has driven up energy prices as the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed.

According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was about $4.30 Monday afternoon, with that same gallon worth about $3.04 last year. In Texas, the average price of a gallon of regular gas was about $3.78 Monday afternoon, up from about $2.60 last year.

The Lone Star State is in the midst of a contentious Senate race, in which Democrats are looking to score a long-sought statewide victory. They are facing a positive electoral environment heading into this year’s midterms as the GOP has been weighed down by issues like the Iran war, increased costs of living and President Trump’s sagging approval numbers .

In the poll, 51 percent of likely voters backed Democrat James Talarico, while 49 percent backed Republican Ken Paxton.

The CBS News/YouGov poll took place from Oct. 8-16, featuring 1,492 registered voters in Texas and a margin of error of 3.4 percentage points.

articles.title: Trump renews push to rename New Mexico ‘New America,’ touts higher home values and incomes
articles.summary: President Trump urged New Mexico to rename itself "New America," claiming the change would boost home values and incomes, while taking a swipe at state elections.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is giving New Mexico another branding pitch, urging the state to swap "Mexico" for "America" and suggesting the change could boost everything from home values to state pride. "New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The name would add great value and prestige to the State! Home Values and Incomes would rise, and you would be even prouder while saluting our beautiful American Flag!" The president also worked in a swipe at the state’s elections. AFTER 'LAKE AMERICA,' TRUMP SUGGESTS A NEW NAME FOR THE STATE OF NEW MEXICO "Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!" he wrote. MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY Trump offered no evidence in the post to support his election allegation or explain how a name change would increase property values and incomes. The suggestion revives an idea Trump floated last month, when he shared a map showing "Mexico" crossed out in red and replaced with "America." The White House amplified that post on its official X account. TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT Trump also pitched the change during remarks at the RNC Midterm Convention on Sept. 9, suggesting neighboring New Mexico become "New America" and claiming the idea was popular. "You have a neighboring state, New Mexico. We think it should be called New America," Trump said. "I’ll tell you, the people love the idea." "I don’t know about the radical left. I’m sure it doesn’t like it, but the people love it," he added. New Mexico’s Democratic governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, pushed back at the time, telling Fox News Digital that the state’s name "isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed." She accused the White House of focusing on a distraction while her administration worked on child care, education, health care and housing. NEW YORK GOV HOCHUL REJECTS TRUMP'S 'LAKE AMERICA' RENAMING WITH BLUNT MESSAGE "While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work," Lujan Grisham said last month. Trump’s latest post calls for the state to change its name but does not lay out a formal process for doing so. New Mexico’s name is expressly written into Article I of its constitution, which states, "The name of this state is New Mexico." HOUSE DEM DEBBIE DINGELL PLACES TRUMP'S LAKE ONTARIO NAME CHANGE IN THE CROSSHAIRS The proposal follows Trump’s moves to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" for federal use and the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America." Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) would be “ashamed” of President Trump’s action Friday to waive sanctions against Russia, less than a month after Trump signed a tough Russia sanctions package into law. Cassidy vented his disappointment with Trump over his decision to set aside sanctions…
articles.body:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) says former President Reagan and the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) would be “ashamed” of President Trump’s action Friday to waive sanctions against Russia, less than a month after Trump signed a tough Russia sanctions package into law.

Cassidy vented his disappointment with Trump over his decision to set aside sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime and its top allies by circulating a critical Wall Street Journal editorial, titled: “To Russia with Love, signed Donald.”

“Reagan and Lindsey would be ashamed of this,” Cassidy wrote above a repost of the Journal’s editorial, featuring a photo of Trump shaking Putin’s hand with Air Force One in the background.

The Journal, which is part of the Murdoch family’s media empire, wrote that “Trump’s assistance to Vladimir Putin keeps growing by the day” and called his decision to waive sanctions “a shiv in the back of the legacy of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.”

The editorial noted that Trump’s executive order waives new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, government entities, financial institutions, the energy industry and the shadow fleet of ships used by Russia to evade international sanctions.

It argued “the evidence compounds that Mr. Trump wants Ukraine to surrender on Mr. Putin’s terms,” pointing out that Trump has dropped sanctions on Russian diesel, has threatened to cut off U.S. intelligence to Kyiv and hasn’t fully explained the impositions on data speed limits on SpaceX’s Starshield network.

“Mr. Trump may not appreciate the anger he’s courting if he keeps aiding Mr. Putin. When the election is over there needs to be a bipartisan reckoning for Mr. Trump’s budding alliance with the Kremlin against Ukraine, Europe and American interests,” the Journal warned.

The publication declared that Trump “is now Mr. Putin’s best friend in the world, after perhaps China’s Xi Jinping.”

Other Republicans have spoken out against Trump’s treatment of Ukraine in recent weeks and the surprising announcement Friday that the administration would waive tough new Russia sanctions.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) blasted Trump and his advisers for ignoring the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which passed the Senate 86-11 in August and which Trump signed last month.

“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis posted Saturday on social platform X.

Tillis is one of four Republican senators who signed a bipartisan letter last week to Department of Defense Inspector General Platte Moring demanding an immediate investigation into whether senior Pentagon officials ordered or had advance knowledge of a decision to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, which it needs to operate drones and other military vehicles.

GOP Sens. John Cornyn (Texas), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Susan Collins (Maine) also signed the letter.

Six Republican senators, including Sens. Mitch McConnell (Ky.) and Alan Armstrong (Okla.), also signed a letter to Trump last week condemning his decision to allow Russia to sell billions of tons of diesel to the United States, in possibly violation of a 2022 law expressly prohibiting the United States from buying Russian energy products without prior notification to Congress.

articles.title: Trump signs order launching women’s health division at NIH, White House
articles.summary: First Lady Melania Trump has championed the executive action as a ‘transformative moment’ for US women’s health.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that will establish a dedicated women’s health division within the National Institutes of Health (NIH), as well as a White House task force focused on the subject.

During a signing ceremony in Washington on Monday, First Lady Melania Trump praised the initiative as setting “a new standard for women’s health in America”.

“This is a transformative moment for women in America. Beginning today, we will change the reality of women’s health,” she said.

“Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”

The newly minted project, spearheaded by the first lady, requires the new health division to be established within 90 days.

It aims to accelerate scientific discoveries, expand clinical access for women’s health and modernise care throughout every stage of a woman’s life.

The new division at the NIH will not replace the agency’s Office of Research on Women’s Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research, according to the White House.

Melania Trump gestured to “super intelligence, advanced biotechnology and groundbreaking therapies” as tools that offer a “unique chance to reinvent women’s healthcare”.

The first lady’s office has identified “five pillars” for innovation in the field. One involves funding targeted research to develop cures for diseases that affect women, such as endometriosis.

Another calls for a quicker timeline for “promising therapeutics” to reach female patients.

“In 2026, medical advances can do more than just prolong life,” said Melania Trump. “It should give women the freedom to live life to its fullest, to pursue our dreams, experience love, discover, create, travel and lead.”

The White House task force will be co-chaired by the newly cancer-free White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, as well as Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.

While Monday’s executive order mandates that the HHS must fund the administrative costs of the task force, the order itself does not include any specific funding targets or dollar amounts.

Experts have noted that Melania Trump has kept a relatively low profile during Trump’s second term.

Her public appearances have been fewer than during Trump’s first term, though she has stepped into the public spotlight to promote improvements to foster care and the role of technology, such as artificial intelligence in education.

During Trump’s first term, the first lady launched the “Be Best” campaign focused on child well-being, safe social media and countering opioid abuse.

But critics have questioned how effective Monday’s executive order might be, given the cuts Trump has made to the federal workforce since his second inauguration.

Thousands of employees have been laid off at the NIH alone, with Kaiser Health News reporting that its workforce is at its lowest level in decades.

The NIH was also given a deadline to slash spending by 35 percent across all of its divisions, amounting to a massive $2.6bn budget reduction.

In April 2025, the HHS drew widespread condemnation and a multi-state lawsuit after abruptly moving to terminate regional contracts for the Women’s Health Initiative, the nation’s largest longitudinal study on older women’s health at the time.

Critics warned that the move would jeopardise life-saving research on cardiovascular disease, cancer and osteoporotic fractures for senior women.

articles.title: How the midterms will shape 2028 and beyond: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur explains why the results of the midterms will have reverberations long after President Donald Trump is out of office.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur explains why the results of the midterms will have reverberations long after President Donald Trump is out of office. Plus, we look at a long-running GOP streak that is at risk next month. — Adam Wollner How the midterms will shape 2028 and beyond Analysis by Sahil Kapur The winners of Congress in the 2026 midterms will wield power to shape the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term, from his legislative agenda to his administrative and judicial appointees. But the outcome of next month’s election will reverberate well beyond the Trump presidency, carrying enormous consequences for his successor in the White House. Beyond which party controls the two chambers, the margins will also matter. Start with the Senate. The winners will be elected to six-year terms, meaning they’ll serve through January 2033, or the end of the next president’s first term. If Democrats manage to win in GOP-leaning states like Texas, Alaska and Iowa — as polls indicate they might — the impact would endure well beyond Trump. And if Republicans fail to hold even redder states like Kansas or Nebraska, that would significantly narrow their path to recapturing the Senate in 2028, even if they have a strong year. The 2028 Senate map will require Democrats to defend seats in Arizona, Georgia, Nevada and Pennsylvania. Republicans failed to capture those seats in a favorable midterm environment in 2022, so it’ll be even more challenging to win them in a presidential cycle while they control the White House. In addition, the GOP will have to defend seats in purple states like North Carolina and Wisconsin that year. (This year’s Ohio Senate race is an exception because it’s a special election for a two-year term, so the seat will come before voters again in 2028.) Conversely, if Republicans are able to hold onto red states that Trump won three times, and protect the seat of Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, or pull off an upset in a purple state like Michigan, where former Rep. Mike Rogers faces Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, they could put Democrats in a jam for 2028. In the modern era, it’s almost unheard of for a new president to enter office without his party controlling both the White House and Senate. The last president to move into the Oval Office under divided government was George H.W. Bush in 1989. In the modern era of polarization — with the two parties far apart on priorities, and the Senate’s power to block Cabinet appointees — it could stymie any new president and put an early dagger in most of his or her legislative agenda. It could also hinder their ability to appoint Supreme Court justices. In the House, where all 435 members are elected to two-year terms, the consequences next month are more immediate. Still, recent history suggests the 2026 midterms carry important consequences for 2028 and beyond. Opposition parties tend to do better in the House in midterm years than the ensuing presidential election. In 2022, Republicans captured the House and then lost a few seats in the 2024 election. In 2018, Democrats captured the House and then lost seats in 2020. In 2010 and 2014, Republicans won the House majority only to lose seats in the subsequent presidential elections of 2012 and 2016. In other words, if Democrats fail to capture the House majority or win it narrowly in 2026, history tells us their power would be in danger two years later. But if they run up the score and flip Republican-held seats, it would give them a cushion in 2028. The last time a party out of power gained House seats in both a midterm and the subsequent presidential election was the Democrats in 2006 and 2008, following one wave cycle with one that took place under the unusual circumstances of a once-in-a-century financial crash. The bottom line: Every seat that Republicans successfully defend in the Senate and the House — even if they lose control of both chambers — could pay off in two years’ time. 🗳️Related read: A blue-collar bellwether weighs ousting longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, by Bridget Bowman Trump and Republicans fight to protect the midterms’ most surprising battleground By Brennan Leach, Stephanie Gosk and Jacob Cavaiani NEWTON, Kansas — No state has shut out one party in U.S. Senate races for as long as Kansas. But with days to go in the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump is headlining a rally near Wichita today in a bid to head off the biggest threat in years to the GOP’s local winning streak. Megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton is hoping to make history as the first Democrat elected to the Senate in ruby-red Kansas in nearly a century. And Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is fighting for his political life in a state he won by over 11 points in 2020, with polls showing a toss up race between Hamilton and the incumbent. Early voting is already underway as Trump heads to the state, which he has carried by at least 14 points three times. But Hamilton has painted Marshall as a “yes man” for the president, in a race that has been defined by the unpopularity of some of Trump’s actions, from high diesel prices hurting farmers to Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids throughout the state. Kansas is one of several reliably red states from recent elections that Democrats have put in play this year as they try to net four seats to take control of the Senate. Wint Winter Jr., a former GOP state senator who is backing Hamilton but remains a registered Republican, told NBC News it wouldn’t surprise him “at all” if Hamilton “won and won big.” “He epitomizes that kind of thinking — how can we do things different?” Winter said. “How can we be thoughtful and kind and open-minded to our opponents?” Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.body:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) accused Mike Davis, a close legal ally of the president, of “mobilizing death threats” against her and her staff.

Slotkin wrote on social media Monday that Davis had originally been in the mix to be President Trump’s next attorney general after former Attorney General Pam Bondi left her post but “is now at a MAGA dark money group, mobilizing death threats against me and my staff for sport.”

“And if you use the justice system for frivolous lawsuits used to intimidate and jail your political opponents, you should be held accountable for that via your bar status. No abuse of power and not violating the law? Then we have no problem,” she continued.

“The threats and intimidation — of me, my staff, and my family — *are the point* of this kind of play. This dude and so many others are just hoping that we’ll shut up in response,” Slotkin wrote.

The senator has received criticism recently from Trump and other figures on the right over remarks she made during an event last week at the University of Chicago, where she said she wanted young people who are considering working for the Trump administration to think, “Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want and so let me avoid participating in that.”

“I want that deterrence message,” she said.

Davis responded to Slotkin’s remarks over the weekend, writing on social media that the Democrat “will learn why we have the Second Amendment” if she employed “illegal arrests and political persecutions to intimidate young Americans with opposing political views.”

“Learn about the Second Amendment, sweetheart,” he wrote in another post Sunday.

Trump additionally called Slotkin “a lowlife” who is “destroying her state” to reporters Monday, accusing Democrats of “really discouraging people from going into politics.”

Davis previously served as chief counsel for nominations to Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) during Trump’s first term, where he cleared the way for the president’s nominees.

Since then, Davis grew closer to Trump during the FBI’s raid of Mar-a-Lago when he defended the president in the press. He also backed the Trump administration’s probe into former Obama-era officials last year, saying on Fox News: “It doesn’t get more serious than this. This is a criminal conspiracy.”

“The evidence is clear there’s a criminal conspiracy here and nobody is above the law,” Davis told Fox News at the time.

He now spearheads Article III Project, a group which says it “brings brass knuckles to fight leftist lawfare,” according to its website .

articles.title: Texas Democratic candidate for governor sues to review emails between Elon Musk and Greg Abbott
articles.summary: State Rep. Gina Hinojosa alleged in her lawsuit that Gov. Greg Abbott is “unlawfully withholding communications” between his office and tech CEO Elon Musk.
articles.body: Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor, announced a lawsuit Monday against Gov. Greg Abbott over emails between his office and Republican ally Elon Musk. Hinojosa — who is challenging Abbott in a tight contest — said at a news conference that she filed the suit to obtain redacted documents that “Abbott refused to release,” claiming they were being withheld because they are “intimate and embarrassing.” A spokesperson for Abbott called the lawsuit “baseless” and “nothing more than an act of desperation.” “Even worse, State Representative Gina Hinojosa is abusing her official capacity as an outgoing lawmaker to generate headlines for political purposes,” Abbott’s press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, said in a statement. “Texans see this for what it is: a political stunt.” Musk, who is CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Hinojosa’s lawsuit alleges the “documented connections between Abbott and Musk are extensive,” including “personal interactions, joint public appearances, large political contributions, economic-development incentives, and public praise for one another.” She claims that Abbott and Musk speak “frequently” and that Musk has “contributed approximately $366 million to Republicans and Republican-supported PACs,” including “large amounts, directly and indirectly, to help Abbott.” It also details the millions of grant dollars given to SpaceX for its operations in Texas, Musk’s home state. Musk in recent months has donated about $250 million to Republican groups, much of it finding its way into Texas races. Hinojosa filed a public information request last month for inspection of all documents exchanged between Abbott’s office and Musk and his companies. In a Sept. 29 letter addressed to the governor’s office, she said the people of Texas are “concerned over the growing power of tech giants in Texas regarding our tax dollars, resources, and data.” Her request followed the release of nearly 1,400 pages of records to The Texas Newsroom, detailed in its 2025 reporting. However, “all but about 200 were redacted or completely blacked out,” according to Monday’s lawsuit. Abbott’s office responded to Hinojosa’s request for the records last Tuesday but “refused to release the unredacted versions,” according to court documents. “Quite simply, Governor Abbott has failed and refused to comply with the law by allowing Representative Hinojosa access to the Abbott-Musk communications,” the lawsuit reads. Hinojosa’s attorney, Cris Feldman, said the governor’s office “has continued to obstruct her ability to review these intimate and embarrassing emails, despite clear statutory language.” In an affidavit, Hinojosa said she seeks the records for “legislative purposes.” She said at the news conference, “The people have a right to know, and I, as their representative, have a right to see them.” Early voting began in Texas on Monday. Hinojosa said she has already cast her ballot.

articles.body:
Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.) on Saturday called out her fellow Democrats over their association with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

“As Democrats, we constantly criticize the far-right for their incendiary and discriminatory politics, but we need to hold ourselves to the same standard,” Craig said in a post on the social platform X . “Hasan Piker’s rhetoric is polarizing and dangerous, and embracing him as a party is a mistake.”

“I am disappointed that Minnesota DFLers are hosting an event with him here,” she added, referencing the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, Minnesota’s equivalent of a Democratic state party.

Piker responded to Craig in his own X post, saying that “another democrat joins the chorus of right wing neo-nazis to attack their left flank.”

“great. this constant desperation to appease the right is precisely why we’re in this mess to begin with,” added Piker, a consistent critic of the Democratic Party.

Piker has become a lightning rod in American politics in the last year. The Twitch streamer also has a history of association with left-leaning figures in American politics, including Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.).

Piker has also earned the ire of more moderate Democrats, including Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.) and Rep. Jared Moskowitz (Fla.).

The streamer’s controversial comments include him saying in 2019 that “America deserved 9/11” due to its military campaigns worldwide. However, he recently said he could have better phrased his comments about the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

articles.title: The Senate map driving Trump’s late-stage travel blitz
articles.summary: President Trump’s focus with two weeks to go before the midterms is squarely on the Senate, as he travels to a series of red states, some of which are threatening to turn blue. The president’s travel schedule has included stops in states seen as deep red such as Alabama, Oklahoma and Tennessee, as well as…
articles.body:
President Trump’s focus with two weeks to go before the midterms is squarely on the Senate, as he travels to a series of red states, some of which are threatening to turn blue.

The president’s travel schedule has included stops in states seen as deep red such as Alabama, Oklahoma and Tennessee, as well as states such as Texas and Kansas where Democratic Senate candidates are in toss-up races.

The president is often giving nods to House campaigns during his travels, but he’s avoiding swing districts for red congressional spots.

That reflects the GOP’s focus on the Senate, where the majority is seen as anyone’s game, in contrast with the House majority, which many Republicans acknowledge will be tough to save.

“That is the conventional wisdom: the House is gone. It’s: protect the Senate with a possible expanding map,” one Republican strategist said.

According to projections by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s partner, the GOP has just a 23 percent chance of winning the House majority. The Senate is more of a coin flip that slightly favors Democrats, who have a 56 percent chance of winning the majority compared with a 44 percent chance for Republicans, per DDHQ.

Trump on Monday embarks on his busiest campaign travel week of the election cycle yet, with stops scheduled in Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan.

One Republican official noted that the party has placed an emphasis on Senate races, saying that much of where Trump is going is decided by where Republicans believe he can best boost statewide turnout.

The president will rally in Wichita, Kan., Monday to boost incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) before he heads to Greenville, N.C., to campaign for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley on Tuesday.

The North Carolina visit shows Trump hasn’t forgotten the House.

Greenville is in North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District, which is considered a safe Republican district. However, it borders the state’s highly competitive 1st Congressional district where Republican Laurie Buckhout is challenging incumbent Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

On Wednesday, Trump will rally in deep-red Clemson, S.C., where Sen. Darlene Graham (R) is defending her seat from Democrat Annie Andrews. The president will visit another competitive Senate state Thursday when he rallies in Sioux City, Iowa, for Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa).

“I think the location for some of President Trump’s rallies do speak more to concerns about the Senate,” said Geoffrey Skelley, DDHQ’s chief elections analyst.

He pointed to Trump’s Sioux City stop, where Iowa’s 4th Congressional District is not considered competitive, as an example.

“That’s basically the reddest part of Iowa is the western part of the state,” Skelley said. “And so, if you’re concerned about Republican base turnout, it’s a place where President Trump could be used very strategically to try to encourage some frustrated Republican voters, or you know, maybe less attuned Republican voters, to go out and cast a ballot in a very important Senate race.”

Trump will head to Florida on Friday, which is home to a Senate race and what appears to be an increasingly competitive gubernatorial race. The city he is set to campaign in, Naples, is a Republican stronghold and home to the party’s gubernatorial nominee Rep. Byron Donalds.

On Saturday, Trump will travel to Georgia’s red-leaning 8th Congressional District to galvanize support for Senate nominee Rep. Mike Collins and gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson. The president will then head to Michigan to campaign for GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers in the state’s 9th Congressional District, which is home to House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Lisa McClain (R).

“Republicans are thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent,” said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary at the Republican National Committee. “The president is barnstorming the country in strategic areas and pouring resources into battleground races to tout his historic achievements, giving Republicans a boost to defy history in November.”

While Trump’s focus appears to be on Senate races, he has taken trips to a number of competitive House districts.

Earlier this month, Trump held a rally for New York GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman in Syracuse, N.Y., which is in the state’s 22nd Congressional District. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the district as “solid Democrat.”

The president also made a stop in San Antonio to rally support for Republican candidate Carlos De La Cruz in the newly redrawn district, which the Cook Political Report rates as “lean Republican.”

And while Trump’s trip to Kentucky on Saturday took place in the state’s GOP-leaning 4th Congressional District, the event was only roughly 7 miles from Cincinnati, Ohio, home to another fiercely competitive Senate race.

“I feel good,” Trump said of his midterm outlook Monday, adding that “a lot of the polls are rigged.”

“I’m the one that’s doing the rallies, that’s taking people into a winning position,” the president told reporters on the South Lawn.

“When you take a look at what’s happened since I’ve been doing these massive, totally sold-out rallies, nobody’s ever seen anything like it,” he said.

A White House official noted that Trump has also used rallies to tout the administration’s accomplishments for the regions he’s visited, as well as their proximity to neighboring media markets.

“With finite resources, he is going places where he can make the biggest impact. President Trump’s message and wins resonate everywhere, and the president wants to communicate with all voters,” the official said.

Republicans “need a major polling error to have a shot” at the House this fall, Skelley said.

Democrats are now considered likely to flip the House and win a 235-200 seat advantage over Republicans, according to the latest DDHQ forecasts. In the Senate, Democrats are narrowly favored to win a 51-49 seat majority.

Against that highly competitive backdrop, Trump’s approval rating is now roughly 20 points underwater , according to DDHQ’s tracker, amid voter frustration with his handling of the economy, the war in Iran and immigration.

Though Trump has urged Republican voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and boost turnout in November, the president’s problematic polling numbers have raised questions for some vulnerable Republicans about just how helpful his campaign trail stops are.

“He’s certainly not welcomed in swing states and even some of these red states. He can be problematic sometimes,” the Republican strategist said.

In audio leaked this month to The New York Times , Texas Senate hopeful Ken Paxton said Republicans’ “Trump-a-palooza” midterm convention in Dallas “dropped our numbers.”

Experts have cautioned that Trump’s recent stops in states such as Texas and ruby-red Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn is battling incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (R), could end up energizing Democrats and independents to turn out against them.

“It took, I think, the Iran conflict to really, really juice this up to a point where Democrats could have a shot because the gas price situation just really, it just really it just exacerbates what was already a lot of economic frustration,” Skelley said.

“Democrats are in this position where they could actually pull it off.”

Interior will hold first offshore mining lease sale

The Trump administration is officially moving ahead with a decision to lease ocean tracts off the coast of American Samoa for deep-sea mining.

© Fili Sagapolutele, Associated Press file

The decision, announced Monday , would represent the first time the U.S. government has offered up offshore mining leases.

Large-scale deep-sea mining has never been done before, but the seafloor could contain valuable minerals, and the administration is making nearly 32 million acres available for companies to bid on in the hopes of extracting them.

The Trump administration has sought to expand mining both onshore and in the ocean, with the president signing an executive order last year to jump-start the deep-sea mining process.

The lease sale will be held on Nov. 19. Companies that win bids would be authorized to conduct preliminary activities like mapping but would not be automatically allowed to start mining.

Dems float Hegseth’s ouster in lame-duck defense battle

Senate Democrats are quietly floating the ouster of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after the midterms as t he political price for cooperation on key defense-related issues in the postelection lame-duck session.

© Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press

The Defense Department has set recruiting records under Hegseth’s leadership, and the Pentagon chief appears to have strong support from President Trump, who likes to brag that Hegseth looks like a military leader from “central casting.”

But the Democrats may have some GOP support to shake up the Pentagon’s leadership, according to Senate sources.

Some Republican senators haven’t been happy with Hegseth’s leadership , especially his ouster of well-respected military leaders such as Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Army chief of staff Randy George, Navy Secretary John Phelan and four-star Gen. Chris Donahue, the top U.S. military officer in Europe.

Democrats view Hegseth’s leadership as a disaster and are looking for leverage to push him out after the midterm elections, according to Senate sources, just as they attempted to push former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem out of her job during the prolonged stalemate over funding for her department earlier this year.

Trump eventually fired Noem after key Republican senators, such as Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), turned against her publicly .

Now Democrats have significant leverage over Hegseth’s future at the Pentagon as they’re threatening to hold up emergency defense funding the White House requested in June as well as regular funding for the Defense Department, which expires on Dec. 11.

My colleague Alexander Bolton spoke with his Democratic and Republican sources on Capitol Hill, where there are growing questions about whether Trump and Hegseth are fully in sync on several important issues.

articles.body:
President Trump called on New Mexico to change its name to “New America” following his decision to alter the names of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario to include “America.”

“New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America,” the president wrote Monday on Truth Social . “The name would add great value and prestige to the State! Home Values and Incomes would rise, and you would be even prouder while saluting our beautiful American Flag!”

“Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again,” he added.

This marked another move by Trump to rename the state after he shared a map to Truth Social last month showing a large “X” over “Mexico” in the state’s name, with the word “America” written below it. The official White House account reposted the image to social platform X.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) wrote on social media Monday that “New Mexico’s name dates back hundreds of years, long before the United States even existed. It carries generations of history, culture, and rich traditions that continue to shape who we are.”

“We are New Mexicans. We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico,” he continued.

Deb Haaland, the Democratic candidate in New Mexico’s gubernatorial race who previously served as Interior secretary under former President Biden, told Trump on social media that he “should be focused on ending this war, stopping these tariffs, and making things less expensive–not renaming our state.”

Trump also passed an executive order in August seeking to change Lake Ontario’s name to “ Lake America ” amid his tariff war with Canada

Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca at the time called on Trump to rescind the order, saying the renaming violated the terms of the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua , which laid out the Seneca Nation’s boundaries as “beginning on Lake Ontario.”

Trump also said he was “ thinking of ” renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean while at a campaign rally in Tennessee earlier this month.

Trump establishes new women’s health divisions

President Trump on Monday signed an executive order creating new executive offices dedicated to bolster research into women’s health , crediting first lady Melania Trump for pushing the issue.

“Today we’re taking historic action to promote women’s health through all phases of life, despite amazing advances in medical science, many diseases and conditions that disproportionately affect women remain chronically understudied,” President Trump said when announcing the order.

The order establishes the Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a White House Women’s Health Task Force .

The task force will be led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr .

Speaking from the White House’s Rose Garden, Melania Trump said the order “establishes a new standard for women’s health in America.”

“Our mission must serve women at every stage of life, from young girls just starting out, to mothers dealing with a complex range of responsibilities, to mature women who deserve to have vitality, dignity and independence,” she said.

According to a fact sheet from the White House, more research is needed in parts of women’s health like Alzheimer’s disease, endometriosis, polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome, infertility, maternal health and menopause.

Some women’s health programs faced potential funding losses shortly after the second Trump administration began.

Early last year, NIH moved to cut funding to the Women’s Health Initiative program, a decades long national health study, to align with a mandate to $2.6 billion in NIH contracts. The decision was ultimately reversed.

articles.title: More than 100K Ukrainians and Sudanese granted temporary deportation reprieve from the U.S.
articles.summary: More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire Monday.
articles.body: MIAMI — More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire Monday. Temporary Protected Status was set to end Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time.” Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the U.S. covered by those temporary measures “retain protection.” The Department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status. DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect. A relief without details The decision Monday marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long. Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a nonprofit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the U.S., described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches.” It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for U.S. to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko added. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine. Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington think tank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said. “It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them." The context of the decisions to keep the protections The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9. In that case, they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the U.S. Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia. Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026. The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive U.S. administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation. The decision Monday comes two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box. The TPS program has offered protections for decades but is controversial The U.S. Congress created TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. It allows people already in the country to remain and work, for renewable periods if the homeland security secretary determines conditions are unsafe for their return. But it doesn't give them a pathway to permanent residency. Supporters say that using this tool protects people from being returned to dangerous situations and that uprooting people covered by TPS after years of living in the U.S. is cruel. Critics, especially in the Trump administration, say successive administrations have extended these protections for years regardless of what has happened in the home countries. Federal rules say TPS is automatically extended for six months if the secretary doesn’t make a determination at least 60 days before the designation expires. Advocates are grateful for DHS decision, warn about the war Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, noted Ukraine and Sudan meet the legal conditions for TPS to be extended. “It is not safe for these families to go home,” Vignarajah said.

articles.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed brought up a Midwestern college rivalry in an attack against Vice President Vance.

During a recent town hall on CBS News, Vance said that he had seen “what Abdul El-Sayed says about the war in Iran.”

“I see he — criticizing decisions that the president has made, the military’s made. But fundamentally, we are where we are, and you have to — in my view, I’d like to know, what is Abdul El-Sayed’s solution for the problem that we have right now?” Vance added.

CNN’s Laura Coates asked El-Sayed about Vance’s comments in a Sunday night interview, to which the Michigan Democrat responded, “first of all, Ohio State [University] owes that boy a refund, because he clearly didn’t get anything from his education there.”

“And, the thing we should not have done is started the war in the first place. In fact, we were in a state of peace with the potential for nuclear proliferation to be contained under the JCPOA under President Obama,” El-Sayed added, referencing the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, the nuclear deal the Obama administration struck with Iran .

Vance attended Ohio State University for his undergraduate degree, while El-Sayed went to the University of Michigan for his. The two Midwestern schools have a notably fierce rivalry.

El-Sayed is facing former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the race for a Senate seat in the Wolverine State, a notable swing state in the battle for the midterms this year. President Trump won Michigan in the 2024 presidential election .

The Cook Political Report rates the Rogers and El-Sayed race as a “toss-up,” but the electoral environment is quite favorable for Democrats this year, with issues like concern around energy costs, the cost of living, Trump’s approval rating and the war in Iran weighing on the GOP as Election Day inches closer.
